lead: A multimedia database stores each item's metadata and a small feature vector. Metadata answers exact questions such as date or owner. Content-based retrieval answers similarity questions: show images like this one. The user gives an example, the system extracts features, compares them by a distance, and ranks the nearest items. This is how photo apps find a face, video archives find a scene, and digital libraries find a slide by colour or shape. The database design matters because comparing every stored item is too slow; indexes make similarity search practical.
prereq: You need: Unit 4 (image and audio features, MPEG-7 overview) and 6.1.

sections.h3: Metadata search and query by example

blocks.text: Every multimedia item enters the database with metadata: title, owner, date, place, format, duration and keywords. A metadata query is exact or Boolean. 'Find lectures recorded after 2024' or 'find files owned by the design team' uses rows in a table, not pixels. This is fast and predictable, but it cannot answer 'find images that look like this sunset'.

Content-based retrieval, also called query by example, takes the user's item as the question. The system extracts a feature vector from the query and from every stored item, then ranks stored items by similarity. The vector is short: a colour histogram, texture numbers, shape descriptors, video key-frame features or audio short-term spectra. A feature is a measurement, not a compressed copy. The original file stays in storage; the database keeps the vector beside the metadata.

Two consequences follow. First, a good feature must survive small changes such as cropping, scaling or re-encoding. Second, retrieval is approximate by design: the answer is a ranked list, not a single true row. The user sees the top k items, where k is the number returned.

For images, a colour histogram counts how much of each colour bin is present. It ignores position, so a rotated image gives the same histogram. Texture describes local variation, for example using edge density or co-occurrence statistics. Shape uses boundaries or region descriptors. For video, key frames summarise shots; for audio, short-term spectra summarise small time windows. These features are chosen because they are compact and can be compared quickly.

Three distance or similarity measures are common. The L1 distance adds absolute differences. The Euclidean distance adds squared differences and takes the square root. Cosine similarity compares direction and ignores length.
d₁(x, y) = Σᵢ |xᵢ − yᵢ|,   d₂(x, y) = √(Σᵢ (xᵢ − yᵢ)²),   cos θ = (x·y) / (‖x‖ ‖y‖)
blocks.where: x and y are feature vectors with components xᵢ and yᵢ; i runs from 1 to n, where n is their length; d₁ is the L1 distance; d₂ is the Euclidean distance; θ is the angle between x and y; x·y = Σᵢ xᵢyᵢ; ‖x‖ = √(Σᵢ xᵢ²). For d₁ and d₂ smaller means more similar; for cos θ larger means more similar.

blocks.text: For L1 and Euclidean, smaller means more similar. For cosine, larger means more similar; the angle θ is between 0 and 90° for non-negative vectors. Histograms are non-negative, so cosine is common in text and audio retrieval.

Checking every stored vector is linear search: for each query, compare with all N items. That is too slow for a library. An index stores vectors so whole regions can be skipped. A k-d tree splits the vector space by one coordinate at a time; it works well for low-dimensional vectors. An R-tree groups nearby objects by minimum bounding rectangles and is common for spatial data and image regions. An inverted file maps a feature value or visual word to the list of items that contain it. High-dimensional vectors weaken tree indexes, so practical systems often combine inverted files with approximate nearest-neighbour search.
Retrieval quality is measured with precision and recall.
precision = R / N_r,   recall = R / N_all
blocks.where: R is the number of relevant items returned; N_r is the total number of items returned; N_all is the total number of relevant items in the database.

blocks.text: Precision asks: of the items returned, how many are relevant? Recall asks: of all relevant items, how many did we return? A system that returns one safe item has high precision and low recall; a system that returns everything has high recall and low precision.

Image retrieval uses colour, texture and shape. Video retrieval uses key frames plus motion or audio. Digital libraries use metadata for catalogue search and content-based retrieval for slides, maps, photographs and recorded lectures. MPEG-7 is a standard for describing media: it defines description schemes for metadata and low-level features so different systems can exchange them. It is not a compression standard; compression belongs to MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and MPEG-4.

figure.caption: The feature index is the fast lookup step. The index box is highlighted because it is what makes retrieval faster than comparing every stored item.

examples.question: A multimedia database stores four-bin colour histograms that sum to 1. The query histogram is q = [0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10]. Image A has h_A = [0.50, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10]; image B has h_B = [0.10, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50]. (a) Compute the L1 distance from q to each image and rank them. (b) The system returns 20 images, of which 12 are relevant; the database contains 30 relevant images. Compute precision and recall.
steps: L1(q, A) = 0.10 + 0.10 + 0.00 + 0.00 = 0.20. The histogram scale has no unit.
A has the smaller L1 distance, so A ranks first and B second.
examples.answer: A ranks first with L1 distance 0.20; B has 1.00; precision is 0.60 and recall is 0.40.
examples.check:
q = [0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10]
A = [0.50, 0.20, 0.20, 0.10]
B = [0.10, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50]
dA = sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(q, A))
dB = sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(q, B))
print(f"{dA:.2f}")
print(f"{dB:.2f}")
returned = 20
relevant_returned = 12
relevant_total = 30
print(f"{relevant_returned / returned:.2f}")
print(f"{relevant_returned / relevant_total:.2f}")

traps: Swapping precision and recall: precision looks at what was returned, recall looks at what was missed.
Treating Euclidean distance as L1: Euclidean squares differences before summing and then takes a square root; L1 does not.
Thinking the feature vector is the stored image: the database stores a compact measurement beside metadata, while the original file stays in storage.
Confusing MPEG-7 with compression: MPEG-7 describes media content; MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and MPEG-4 handle compression.
Using cosine as a distance where larger means worse: cosine similarity is larger for more similar vectors, so rank by decreasing cosine.

quiz.q: What is the difference between metadata search and content-based retrieval?
quiz.a: Metadata search matches stored fields exactly or by range; content-based retrieval compares feature vectors and returns a ranked list by similarity.
It standardises descriptions of media content, including metadata and low-level features, so systems can exchange descriptions. It does not compress media.

quiz.q: Why is a feature index needed in a multimedia database?
quiz.a: Comparing the query with every stored vector costs O(N); an index prunes most comparisons and makes top-k retrieval practical.

quiz.q: Using four-bin histograms, compare q = [0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25] with A = [0.40, 0.20, 0.20, 0.20] and B = [0.10, 0.10, 0.30, 0.50] by L1 distance. Which ranks first?
quiz.a: d₁(q,A) = 0.15 + 0.05 + 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.30. d₁(q,B) = 0.15 + 0.15 + 0.05 + 0.25 = 0.60. A ranks first because smaller L1 means more similar.

quiz.q: A search returns 50 images; 20 are relevant. The database has 80 relevant images. Compute precision and recall.
Name one feature for image retrieval and one for audio retrieval, and say what each measures.
quiz.a: A colour histogram measures how much of each colour bin is present. A short-term spectrum measures frequency energy in a small audio window.

quiz.q: Why can two visually similar images have different metadata, and why does that matter for retrieval?
quiz.a: Metadata such as title, owner or date is added by people and may be missing or inconsistent. Content-based retrieval uses pixels-derived features, so it can still find similar images; metadata search would miss them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern systems often replace hand-made features with learned embeddings and store them in vector databases. Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes trade a little recall for large speed gains. Researchers search for robust features that survive cropping, rotation and compression. Useful search terms: content-based image retrieval, vector database, approximate nearest neighbour, CLIP, MPEG-7 description schemes.
